items.new: When, on that shivering winter's night, the Pequod thrust her vengeful bows into the cold, malicious waves, who should I see standing at her helm but Bulkington! I looked at the man with sympathetic awe and dread. Here was someone who, in midwinter, having just landed from a dangerous four-year voyage, could so restlessly push off again for yet another stormy term at sea. The land seemed to scorch his feet. The most wondrous things are always the ones that cannot be spoken; deep memories yield no epitaphs; this six-inch chapter is the stoneless grave of Bulkington. Let me say only that it went with him as with the storm-tossed ship that drives miserably along a lee shore. The port would gladly give shelter; the port is compassionate; in the port there is safety, comfort, a hearth, supper, warm blankets, friends — everything that is kind to our mortal selves. But in that gale, the port, the land, is that ship's direst danger. She must flee all hospitality. One touch of land, even if it only grazed the keel, would make her shudder through and through. With all her might she crowds on every sail to get offshore, and in doing so fights the very winds that would gladly blow her homeward. She seeks the lashed sea's landlessness again, rushing forlornly into danger for the sake of refuge — her only friend her bitterest enemy!

Up from the spray of your ocean death — straight up — leaps your apotheosis!

items.new: No doubt one main reason the world refuses to honor us whalemen is this: people think that, at best, our occupation amounts to a butchering sort of business, and that when we're actively at work, we're surrounded by every kind of filth. Butchers we are — that's true. But butchers, too, and butchers of the bloodiest badge, have been all the military commanders whom the world invariably loves to honor. And as for the alleged uncleanliness of our business, you'll soon be let in on certain facts that until now have been pretty generally unknown, and which, on the whole, will triumphantly place the sperm whale ship at least among the cleanest things on this tidy earth. But even granting the charge to be true — what messy, slippery decks of a whale ship can compare with the unspeakable carrion of those battlefields from which so many soldiers return to drink in the applause of every lady? And if the idea of danger so greatly enhances the popular admiration of the soldier's profession, let me assure you that many a veteran who has freely marched up to a cannon battery would quickly recoil at the sight of a sperm whale's vast tail fanning the air above his head into eddies. For what are the terrors of man, which we can understand, compared with the interlinked terrors and wonders of God!

Why did Louis XVI of France, at his own personal expense, fit out whaling ships from Dunkirk, and politely invite a score or two of families from our own island of Nantucket to that town? Why did Britain, between the years 1750 and 1788, pay her whalemen upwards of £1,000,000 in bounties? And lastly, how is it that we American whalemen now outnumber all the rest of the world's whalemen banded together; sail a navy of upwards of seven hundred vessels, manned by eighteen thousand men, consuming $4,000,000 a year, the ships worth $20,000,000 at the time of sailing; and every year bring into our harbors a well-reaped harvest of $7,000,000? items.new: I freely assert that the cosmopolitan philosopher cannot, for the life of him, point to one single peaceful influence that, within the last sixty years, has worked more powerfully upon the whole broad world, taken all together, than the high and mighty business of whaling. One way and another, it has produced events so remarkable in themselves, and so continuously momentous in their consequences, that whaling may well be regarded as that Egyptian mother who bore offspring that were themselves pregnant from her womb. It would be a hopeless, endless task to catalogue all these things. Let a handful be enough. For many years past the whale ship has been the pioneer in ferreting out the remotest and least known parts of the earth. She has explored seas and archipelagoes that had no chart, where no Cook or Vancouver had ever sailed. If American and European warships now ride peacefully in once savage harbors, let them fire salutes to the honor and glory of the whale ship, which first showed them the way and first interpreted between them and the savages. They may celebrate as they like the heroes of Exploring Expeditions, your Cooks, your Krusensterns; but I say that scores of anonymous captains have sailed out of Nantucket who were as great as your Cook and your Krusenstern, and greater. For in their helpless, empty-handed state, in heathenish, shark-filled waters and by the beaches of unrecorded, javelin-throwing islands, they battled with virgin wonders and terrors that Cook, with all his marines and muskets, would not willingly have dared. All that is made such a flourish of in the old South Sea Voyages was only the lifelong commonplace of our heroic Nantucketers. Often, adventures to which Vancouver devotes three chapters, these men thought unworthy of being set down in the ship's ordinary log. Ah, the world! Oh, the world!

items.new: That great America on the other side of the globe, Australia, was given to the enlightened world by the whaleman. After its first blunder-born discovery by a Dutchman, all other ships long shunned those shores as pestilently barbarous; but the whale ship called there. The whale ship is the true mother of that now mighty colony. Moreover, in the infancy of the first Australian settlement, the emigrants were several times saved from starvation by the benevolent biscuit of a whale ship that luckily dropped anchor in their waters. The countless islands of all Polynesia confess the same truth, and pay commercial homage to the whale ship, which cleared the way for the missionary and the merchant, and in many cases carried the first missionaries to their destinations. If that double-bolted land, Japan, is ever to become hospitable, it is the whale ship alone that will deserve the credit — for she is already on the threshold.

There is a so-called salt cellar of state, and there may be a castor of state, a ceremonial cruet. How exactly they use the salt — who knows? What I am certain of, however, is that a king's head is solemnly oiled at his coronation, just like a head of salad. items.new: The chief mate of the Pequod was Starbuck, a native of Nantucket and a Quaker by descent. He was a long, earnest man, and though born on an icy coast, he seemed well suited to endure hot latitudes, his flesh being as hard as twice-baked biscuit. Carried to the Indies, his living blood would not spoil like bottled ale. He must have been born in some time of general drought and famine, or on one of those fast days for which his state is famous. He had seen only some thirty arid summers, and those summers had dried up everything superfluous in his body. But this thinness of his, so to speak, seemed no more a sign of wasting anxieties and cares than of any bodily disease. It was simply the condensation of the man. He was by no means bad-looking — quite the contrary. His clean, tight skin was an excellent fit; and closely wrapped up in it, and embalmed with inner health and strength, like an Egyptian mummy brought back to life, this Starbuck seemed prepared to endure for long ages to come, and to endure always as he was now. For whether in polar snow or torrid sun, like a patent chronometer, his inner vitality was guaranteed to do well in all climates. Looking into his eyes, you seemed to see there the still-lingering images of the thousandfold dangers he had calmly faced throughout his life. A staid, steadfast man, whose life for the most part was an eloquent pantomime of action, not a tame chapter of sounds. Yet for all his hardy sobriety and fortitude, there were certain qualities in him which at times affected, and in some cases seemed almost to outweigh, all the rest. Uncommonly conscientious for a seaman, and endowed with a deep natural reverence, he was strongly inclined by the wild, watery loneliness of his life toward superstition — but toward that sort of superstition which in some minds seems, somehow, to spring from intelligence rather than from ignorance. Outward omens and inward premonitions were his. And if at times these things bent the welded iron of his soul, much more did his far-away memories of home, of his young Cape Cod wife and child, bend him still further from the original ruggedness of his nature, and open him still further to those hidden influences which, in some honest-hearted men, hold back the gush of daredevil daring so often shown by others in the more dangerous turns of the fishery. "I will have no man in my boat," said Starbuck, "who is not afraid of a whale." By this he seemed to mean not only that the most reliable and useful courage is the kind that arises from a fair estimate of the danger faced, but that an utterly fearless man is a far more dangerous comrade than a coward.

items.new: Starbuck was no crusader after dangers; in him courage was not a sentiment but a thing simply useful to him, and always at hand on every occasion that was practical to the point of life and death. Besides, he thought, perhaps, that in this business of whaling, courage was one of the great staple supplies of the ship, like her beef and her bread, and not to be foolishly wasted. So he had no liking for lowering the boats for whales after sundown, nor for persisting in fighting a whale that persisted too much in fighting him. For, thought Starbuck, I am here on this critical ocean to kill whales for my living, and not to be killed by them for theirs; and Starbuck knew well that hundreds of men had been killed that way. What fate had been his own father's? Where, in the bottomless depths, could he find the torn limbs of his brother?

items.new: With memories like these in him, and given, moreover, to a certain superstitiousness, as has been said, the courage of this Starbuck, which could nevertheless still flourish, must indeed have been extreme. But it was not in reasonable nature that a man built this way, with such terrible experiences and memories as he had — it was not in nature that these things should fail to breed, hidden in him, an element which, under suitable circumstances, would break out of its confinement and burn all his courage up. And brave as he might be, his was chiefly the sort of bravery, seen in some fearless men, which, while generally holding firm in the conflict with seas, or winds, or whales, or any of the ordinary irrational horrors of the world, cannot withstand those more terrible, because more spiritual, terrors which sometimes threaten you from the concentrated brow of an enraged and mighty man.

items.new: But if the coming narrative were to reveal, in any instance, the complete collapse of poor Starbuck's fortitude, I would hardly have the heart to write it; for it is a most sorrowful thing — no, a shocking one — to expose the fall of valor in the soul. Men may seem detestable as joint-stock companies and nations; there may be knaves, fools, and murderers; men may have mean and meager faces; but man, in the ideal, is so noble and so sparkling, such a grand and glowing creature, that over any shameful blemish in him all his fellows should run to throw their costliest robes. That immaculate manliness we feel within ourselves, so far within us that it remains intact even when all the outer character seems gone, bleeds with the keenest anguish at the unrobed spectacle of a man whose valor is ruined. Nor can piety itself, at such a shameful sight, completely stifle her reproaches against the stars that permitted it. But this majestic dignity I speak of is not the dignity of kings and robes, but that abounding dignity which has no robed investiture. You shall see it shining in the arm that wields a pick or drives a spike; that democratic dignity which, on all sides, radiates without end from God — Himself! The great God absolute! The center and circumference of all democracy! His omnipresence, our divine equality!

items.new: Stubb was the second mate. He was a native of Cape Cod, and so, according to local usage, was called a Cape-Cod-man. A happy-go-lucky type; neither cowardly nor valiant; taking dangers as they came with an indifferent air; and in the most urgent crisis of the chase, toiling away, calm and collected as a journeyman carpenter hired for the year. Good-humored, easy, and carefree, he presided over his whale-boat as if the deadliest encounter were only a dinner, and his crew all invited guests. He was as particular about the comfortable arrangement of his part of the boat as an old stagecoach driver is about the snugness of his seat. When close to the whale, in the very death-lock of the fight, he handled his pitiless lance coolly and offhandedly, as a whistling tinker handles his hammer. He would hum his old rigadig tunes while flank to flank with the most furious monster. Long habit had, for this Stubb, turned the jaws of death into an easy chair. What he thought of death itself, there is no telling. Whether he ever thought of it at all might be a question; but if he ever did happen to turn his mind that way after a comfortable dinner, no doubt, like a good sailor, he took it to be a sort of call of the watch to tumble aloft and bestir themselves there, about something he would find out when he obeyed the order, and not sooner.

items.new: What, perhaps, along with other things, made Stubb such an easygoing, unfearing man, so cheerily trudging along with the burden of life in a world full of grave peddlers all bowed to the ground by their packs — what helped to bring about that almost impious good humor of his — that thing must have been his pipe. For, like his nose, his short, black little pipe was one of the regular features of his face. You would almost as soon have expected him to turn out of his bunk without his nose as without his pipe. He kept a whole row of pipes there, ready loaded, stuck in a rack within easy reach of his hand; and whenever he turned in, he smoked them all out one after another, lighting each from the last to the very end; then loaded them again to be ready once more. For when Stubb dressed, instead of first putting his legs into his trousers, he put his pipe into his mouth.

items.new: The third mate was Flask, a native of Tisbury, on Martha's Vineyard. A short, stout, ruddy young fellow, very pugnacious about whales, who somehow seemed to think that the great leviathans had personally and hereditarily insulted him; and therefore it was a sort of point of honor with him to destroy them whenever he met them. So utterly lost was he to all sense of reverence for the many marvels of their majestic bulk and mystic ways, and so dead to anything like a sense of possible danger from encountering them, that in his poor opinion the wondrous whale was only a species of magnified mouse, or at least water rat, requiring only a little outmaneuvering and some small expense of time and trouble in order to kill and boil. This ignorant, unconscious fearlessness of his made him a little waggish on the subject of whales; he followed these fish for the fun of it; and a three-year voyage around Cape Horn was only a jolly joke that lasted that long. As a carpenter's nails are divided into wrought nails and cut nails, so mankind may be divided in the same way. Little Flask was one of the wrought ones, made to clinch tight and last long. They called him King-Post on board the Pequod, because in shape he could well be likened to the short, square timber known by that name in Arctic whalers, which, by means of many radiating side timbers set into it, serves to brace the ship against the icy shocks of those battering seas.

items.new: Next was Tashtego, an unmixed Indian from Gay Head, the westernmost promontory of Martha's Vineyard, where there still exists the last remnant of a village of red men, which has long supplied the neighboring island of Nantucket with many of her most daring harpooners. In the fishery, they usually go by the general name of Gay-Headers. Tashtego's long, lean, sable hair, his high cheekbones, and his black, rounded eyes — for an Indian, Oriental in their largeness, but Antarctic in their glittering expression — all this was enough to proclaim him an heir of the untainted blood of those proud warrior-hunters who, in quest of the great New England moose, had scoured the primeval forests of the mainland, bow in hand. But no longer sniffing the trail of the wild beasts of the woodland, Tashtego now hunted in the wake of the great whales of the sea, the unerring harpoon of the son fittingly replacing the infallible arrow of the fathers. Looking at the tawny brawn of his lithe, snaky limbs, you would almost have credited the superstitions of some of the earlier Puritans, and half-believed this wild Indian to be a son of the Prince of the Powers of the Air. Tashtego was the squire of Stubb, the second mate.

items.new: Third among the harpooners was Daggoo, a gigantic, coal-black negro-savage, with a lion-like tread — an Ahasuerus to behold. Hanging from his ears were two golden hoops, so large that the sailors called them ring-bolts, and would talk of securing the topsail halyards to them. In his youth Daggoo had voluntarily signed aboard a whaler lying in a lonely bay on his native coast. And having never been anywhere in the world but Africa, Nantucket, and the pagan harbors most visited by whalemen, and having now led for many years the bold life of the fishery in the ships of owners unusually careful about what sort of men they shipped, Daggoo kept all his barbaric virtues, and, erect as a giraffe, moved about the decks in all the pomp of six feet five in his socks. There was a bodily humility in looking up at him; and a white man standing before him seemed a white flag come to beg a truce of a fortress. Curious to say, this imperial negro, Ahasuerus Daggoo, was the squire of little Flask, who looked like a chess piece beside him. As for the rest of the Pequod's company, let it be said that at the present day not one in two of the many thousand men before the mast employed in the American whale fishery are American-born, though nearly all the officers are. In this the American whale fishery is the same as the American army and the military and merchant navies, and the engineering forces employed in building the American canals and railroads. The same, I say, because in all these cases the native American liberally provides the brains, and the rest of the world as generously supplies the muscles. No small number of these whaling seamen belong to the Azores, where the outward-bound Nantucket whalers often call to fill out their crews from the hardy peasants of those rocky shores. In the same way, the Greenland whalers sailing out of Hull or London put in at the Shetland Islands to take on their full complement of crew, and on the passage home they drop them there again. How it is, there is no telling, but islanders seem to make the best whalemen. They were nearly all islanders in the Pequod — Isolatoes too, I call such, not acknowledging the common continent of men, but each Isolato living on a separate continent of his own. Yet now, federated along one keel, what a set these Isolatoes were! An Anacharsis Clootz deputation from all the isles of the sea and all the ends of the earth, accompanying old Ahab in the Pequod to lay the world's grievances before that bar from which not very many of them ever come back. Black little Pip — he never did — oh, no! he went before. Poor Alabama boy! On the grim Pequod's forecastle you shall soon see him, beating his tambourine; a prelude to the eternal time when, sent for to the great quarter-deck on high, he was told to strike in with the angels and beat his tambourine in glory; called a coward here, hailed a hero there!

items.reason: "their supreme lord and dictator" became "lord and ruler".
items.new: For several days after leaving Nantucket, nothing was seen of Captain Ahab above the hatches. The mates regularly relieved each other at the watches, and for all that could be seen to the contrary, they seemed to be the only commanders of the ship; only, they sometimes came out of the cabin with orders so sudden and peremptory that it was plain, after all, that they were only commanding on someone else's behalf. Yes, their supreme lord and dictator was there, though so far unseen by any eyes not permitted to penetrate the now sacred retreat of the cabin.

items.reason: Dropped: "the ragged Elijah's diabolical incoherences" (candidate adds "warnings" and loses "diabolical"); "But poorly could I withstand them" overstated as "I couldn't resist them"; "barbaric, heathenish, and motley" softened to "wild, heathen, and mixed"; "tame merchant-ship companies"; "with a fair wind"; "every degree and minute of latitude"; "all its intolerable weather".
items.new: Every time I came up on deck from my watches below, I instantly looked aft to see if any strange face was visible; for my first vague uneasiness about the unknown captain, now in the seclusion of the sea, had become almost an agitation. This was strangely heightened at times by the ragged Elijah's diabolical, incoherent ramblings, which came back to me uninvited, with a subtle energy I could not have imagined before. I could only poorly withstand them, much as in other moods I was almost ready to smile at the solemn whims of that outlandish prophet of the wharves. But whatever apprehension or uneasiness — to call it that — I felt, whenever I came to look around me in the ship, it seemed against all reason to cherish such feelings. For though the harpooners, with the great body of the crew, were a far more barbaric, heathenish, and motley set than any of the tame merchant-ship companies I had known before, I still put this down — and rightly — to the fierce uniqueness of the very nature of that wild Scandinavian calling in which I had so recklessly embarked. But it was above all the look of the three chief officers of the ship, the mates, that was most strongly fitted to allay these colorless misgivings and to inspire confidence and cheerfulness about every prospect of the voyage. Three better, more promising sea-officers and men, each in his own different way, could not easily be found, and every one of them was American: a Nantucketer, a Vineyarder, a Cape man. Now, since it was Christmas when the ship shot out of her harbor, for a while we had biting polar weather, though all the time we were running away from it to the southward; and with every degree and minute of latitude we sailed, we gradually left that merciless winter and all its intolerable weather behind us. It was one of those less lowering, but still gray and gloomy enough, mornings of the transition, when with a fair wind the ship was rushing through the water with a vengeful sort of leaping and melancholy speed, that, as I climbed to the deck at the call of the forenoon watch, the moment I leveled my gaze toward the taffrail at the stern, foreboding shivers ran over me. Reality outran apprehension: Captain Ahab stood upon his quarter-deck.

items.reason: Contradiction introduced: "when the fire has overrunningly wasted all the limbs without consuming them" became "the fire has consumed all his limbs' outer surface without destroying them". "seemed inferentially negatived" lost "inferentially"; "preternatural" became "supernatural".
items.new: There seemed to be no sign of ordinary bodily illness about him, nor of recovery from any. He looked like a man cut down from the stake when the fire has swept over and withered all the limbs without consuming them, or taking away one particle of their compact, aged robustness. His whole tall, broad form seemed made of solid bronze, and shaped in an unalterable mold, like Cellini's cast Perseus. Threading its way out from among his gray hairs, and continuing right down one side of his tawny, scorched face and neck until it disappeared into his clothing, you saw a slender, rod-like mark, livid and whitish. It resembled that vertical seam sometimes made in the straight, lofty trunk of a great tree when the lightning from above darts tearing down it, and, without wrenching off a single twig, peels and grooves out the bark from top to bottom before running off into the soil, leaving the tree still green and alive, but branded. Whether that mark was born with him, or whether it was the scar left by some desperate wound, no one could say for certain. By some unspoken agreement, little or no mention was made of it throughout the voyage, especially by the mates. But once Tashtego's senior, an old Gay-Head Indian among the crew, superstitiously asserted that Ahab was not branded that way until he was a full forty years old, and that it came upon him not in the fury of any mortal fight, but in an elemental struggle at sea. Yet this wild hint seemed, by inference, to be contradicted by what a gray Manxman hinted — an old, sepulchral man who, having never sailed out of Nantucket before, had never until now laid eyes on wild Ahab. Nevertheless, the old sea traditions, the immemorial credulities, popularly credited this old Manxman with preternatural powers of discernment. So no white sailor seriously contradicted him when he said that if Captain Ahab should ever be laid out peacefully — which might hardly come to pass, so he muttered — then whoever performed that last office for the dead would find a birthmark on him from crown to sole.

items.reason: "He has a quiver of 'em" (the arrow-quiver image, several spare legs) became "a whole supply of them".
items.new: So powerfully did the whole grim aspect of Ahab affect me, and the livid brand which streaked it, that for the first few moments I hardly noticed that not a little of this overpowering grimness was owing to the barbaric white leg on which he partly stood. I had heard earlier that this ivory leg had been fashioned at sea from the polished bone of the sperm whale's jaw. "Aye, he was dismasted off Japan," the old Gay-Head Indian once said, "but like his dismasted ship, he shipped another mast without coming home for it. He has a quiver of them."

items.reason: "the warm, warbling persuasiveness" lost "warbling"; "the wintry, misanthropic woods" became "bitter woods"; "the playful allurings of that girlish air" became "gentle air", breaking the April-and-May girls image (same slip type as "butterfly cheeks").
items.new: Nevertheless, before long, the warm, warbling persuasiveness of the pleasant holiday weather we came into seemed gradually to charm him out of his mood. For as when the red-cheeked dancing girls, April and May, come tripping home to the wintry, misanthropic woods, even the barest, most rugged, most thunder-split old oak will at least send out a few green sprouts to welcome such glad-hearted visitors, so Ahab did, in the end, respond a little to the playful enticements of that girlish air. More than once he put forth the faint blossom of a look which, in any other man, would soon have flowered into a smile.

items.reason: Proper name and specifics dropped: "the bright Quito spring" became "spring of the equatorial regions"; "the eternal August of the Tropic" became "eternal summer"; "their absent conquering Earls" became "lords"; "overflowing, redundant days" lost "redundant". Gloss added for Quito (the city on the equator whose climate is a byword for perpetual spring).
items.new: Some days passed, and with ice and icebergs all astern, the Pequod now went rolling through the bright Quito spring — the endless spring of that city on the equator — which at sea reigns almost perpetually on the threshold of the eternal August of the Tropic. The warmly cool, clear, ringing, perfumed, overflowing, abundant days were like crystal goblets of Persian sherbet, heaped up — flaked up — with rose-water snow. The starry, stately nights seemed like haughty ladies in jeweled velvets, nursing at home in lonely pride the memory of their absent conquering Earls, the golden-helmeted suns! For a sleeping man, it was hard to choose between such winsome days and such seductive nights. But all the enchantments of that unfading weather did not merely lend new spells and powers to the outer world. They turned inward upon the soul, especially when the still, mild hours of evening came on; then memory shot out her crystals as clear ice forms most readily in noiseless twilights. And all these subtle influences worked more and more upon the fabric of Ahab.

items.reason: "a globe of tow, and the insertion into it, of the ivory heel" became "inserting it around the ivory heel" (the heel goes into the ball, not the ball around it); "he was measuring the ship from taffrail to mainmast".
items.new: So almost every twenty-four hours, when the night watches were set and the men on deck stood guard over the sleep of the men below; and when, if a rope had to be hauled on the forecastle, the sailors did not fling it down roughly, as by day, but dropped it carefully into its place for fear of disturbing their sleeping shipmates; when this sort of steady quiet would begin to settle in, the silent helmsman would habitually watch the cabin hatch; and before long the old man would emerge, gripping the iron railing to help his crippled way. There was some considerate touch of humanity in him; for at times like these he usually refrained from patrolling the quarter-deck, because to his weary mates, trying to rest within six inches of his ivory heel, the echoing crack and din of that bony step would have been such that their dreams would have been of the crunching teeth of sharks. But once, the mood was on him too deep for ordinary consideration; and as with a heavy, lumbering pace he was measuring the ship from the taffrail to the mainmast, Stubb, the old second mate, came up from below and, with a certain unsure, apologetic humor, hinted that if Captain Ahab was pleased to walk the planks, then no one could say no; but there might be some way of muffling the noise — hinting something vaguely and hesitantly about a ball of tow, and inserting the ivory heel into it. Ah, Stubb, you did not know Ahab then.

items.new: Startled by the unforeseen closing exclamation of the so suddenly scornful old man, Stubb was speechless for a moment; then said excitedly, "I'm not used to being spoken to that way, sir; I like it less than half, sir."

items.reason: "A hot old man!" (the joke on the hot pillow) became "A restless old man!"; "it's a kind of Tic-Dolly-row they say" (Stubb's mangling of tic douloureux, a facial nerve pain) became "a kind of torture"; "his eyes like powder-pans!" (the flash-pan of a gun) became "like gunpowder"; "hammock clothes"; "plaguey juggling".
items.new: "I was never served like that before without giving a hard blow for it," muttered Stubb, as he found himself going down the cabin hatch. "It's very queer. Stop, Stubb; somehow, now, I don't quite know whether to go back and hit him, or — what's that? — get down here on my knees and pray for him? Yes, that was the thought coming up in me; but it would be the first time I ever really did pray. It's queer; very queer; and he's queer too; aye, take him fore and aft, he's about the queerest old man Stubb ever sailed with. How he flashed at me! — his eyes like powder-pans! Is he mad? Anyway, there's something on his mind, as sure as there must be something on a deck when it cracks. He isn't in his bed now, either, more than three hours out of the twenty-four; and he doesn't sleep then. Didn't that Dough-Boy, the steward, tell me that in the morning he always finds the old man's hammock clothes all rumpled and tumbled, and the sheets down at the foot, and the coverlet almost tied into knots, and the pillow a sort of frightful hot, as though a baked brick had been on it? A hot old man! I guess he's got what some folks ashore call a conscience; it's a kind of Tic-Dolly-row, they say — worse than a toothache. Well, well; I don't know what it is, but the Lord keep me from catching it. He's full of riddles; I wonder what he goes into the after hold for every night, as Dough-Boy tells me he suspects; what's that for, I'd like to know? Who's made appointments with him in the hold? Isn't that queer, now? But there's no telling; it's the old game. Here goes for a snooze. Damn me, it's worth a fellow's while to be born into the world, if only to fall right asleep. And now that I think of it, that's about the first thing babies do, and that's sort of queer, too. Damn me, but all things are queer, come to think of them. But that's against my principles. Think not, is my eleventh commandment; and sleep when you can, is my twelfth. So here goes again. But how's that? Didn't he call me a dog? Blazes! He called me ten times a donkey, and piled a lot of jackasses on top of that! He might as well have kicked me, and been done with it. Maybe he did kick me, and I didn't notice it, I was so taken aback by his brow, somehow. It flashed like a bleached bone. What the devil's the matter with me? I don't stand right on my legs. Running afoul of that old man has sort of turned me inside out. By the Lord, I must have been dreaming, though — how? how? how? — but the only way is to stow it; so here goes to the hammock again; and in the morning I'll see how this plaguey hocus-pocus looks when I think it over by daylight."

items.reason: "the binnacle lamp" became "compass lamp"; nautical term restored with the brief gloss.
items.new: When Stubb had gone, Ahab stood for a while leaning over the bulwarks. Then, as had been his habit lately, he called a sailor of the watch and sent him below for his ivory stool, and also his pipe. Lighting the pipe at the binnacle lamp (the lamp by the compass) and planting the stool on the weather side of the deck, he sat and smoked.

items.reason: "a Khan of the plank, and a king of the sea, and a great lord of Leviathans" became "a king of the planks, a lord of the sea, and a great ruler of Leviathans": Khan dropped and the titles reshuffled.
items.new: In old Norse times, the thrones of the sea-loving Danish kings were made, so tradition says, of the tusks of the narwhal. How could anyone look at Ahab then, seated on that tripod of bones, without thinking of the royalty it symbolized? For Ahab was a Khan of the plank, and a king of the sea, and a great lord of Leviathans.

items.reason: "like the dying whale, my final jets were the strongest" became "final gasps" (the spout image lost); the repeated "to windward; to windward" collapsed.
items.new: Some moments passed, during which the thick smoke came from his mouth in quick, constant puffs that blew back into his face. "How now," he said to himself at last, taking the stem from his mouth, "this smoking no longer soothes. Oh, my pipe! Things must be going hard with me if your charm is gone! Here I have been unknowingly toiling, not taking pleasure — aye, and ignorantly smoking to windward all the while; to windward, and with such nervous whiffs, as if, like the dying whale, my final spouts were the strongest and fullest of trouble. What business do I have with this pipe? This thing is meant for serenity, to send up mild white vapors among mild white hairs, not among torn iron-gray locks like mine. I'll smoke no more —"

items.reason: Dropped: the merman's command "be kicked by him"; "let's argue the insult" became "let's think about"; "like a chimney hag" lost "chimney"; "common pitch pine leg"; "there's a devilish broad insult"; "in some queer fashion"; "seaweed he had for a clout".
items.new: "I never had such a queer dream, King-Post. You know the old man's ivory leg? Well, I dreamed he kicked me with it; and when I tried to kick back, upon my soul, my little man, I kicked my leg right off! And then, presto! Ahab seemed to be a pyramid, and I, like a blazing fool, kept kicking at it. But what was still more curious, Flask — you know how curious all dreams are — through all this rage I was in, I somehow seemed to be thinking to myself that, after all, it wasn't much of an insult, that kick from Ahab. 'Why,' thinks I, 'what's the row? It's not a real leg, only a false leg.' And there's a mighty difference between a living thump and a dead thump. That's what makes a blow from the hand, Flask, fifty times more savage to bear than a blow from a cane. The living limb — that's what makes the living insult, my little man. And all the while, mind you, I was thinking to myself, while I was stubbing my silly toes against that cursed pyramid — so confoundedly contradictory was it all — all the while, I say, I was thinking to myself, 'What's his leg now but a cane — a whalebone cane? Yes,' thinks I, 'it was only a playful cudgeling — in fact, only a whaleboning he gave me — not a low kick. Besides,' thinks I, 'just look at it: why, the end of it — the foot part — what a small sort of end it is; whereas if a broad-footed farmer kicked me, now there's a devilish broad insult. But this insult is whittled down to a point.' But now comes the biggest joke of the dream, Flask. While I was battering away at the pyramid, a sort of badger-haired old merman with a hump on his back takes me by the shoulders and swings me round. 'What are you up to?' says he. Lord! man, but I was frightened. Such a mug! But somehow, the next moment I was over the fright. 'What am I up to?' says I at last. 'And what business is that of yours, I'd like to know, Mr. Humpback? Do you want a kick?' By the Lord, Flask, no sooner had I said that than he turned his stern to me, bent over, and, dragging up a lot of seaweed he wore for a loincloth — what do you think I saw? — why, thunder alive, man, his stern was stuck full of marlinspikes, with the points out. Says I, on second thought, 'I guess I won't kick you, old fellow.' 'Wise Stubb,' said he, 'wise Stubb;' and kept muttering it all the time, a sort of chewing on his own gums like an old hag by the chimney. Seeing he wasn't going to stop saying over his 'wise Stubb, wise Stubb,' I thought I might as well go back to kicking the pyramid. But I had only just lifted my foot for it when he roared out, 'Stop that kicking!' 'Hello,' says I, 'what's the matter now, old fellow?' 'Look here,' says he; 'let's argue the insult. Captain Ahab kicked you, didn't he?' 'Yes, he did,' says I — 'right here it was.' 'Very good,' says he — 'he used his ivory leg, didn't he?' 'Yes, he did,' says I. 'Well then,' says he, 'wise Stubb, what have you got to complain of? Didn't he kick with right good will? It wasn't a common pitch-pine leg he kicked with, was it? No, you were kicked by a great man, and with a beautiful ivory leg, Stubb. It's an honor; I consider it an honor. Listen, wise Stubb. In old England the greatest lords think it a great glory to be slapped by a queen and made Knights of the Garter; but let your boast be, Stubb, that you were kicked by old Ahab and made a wise man of. Remember what I say: be kicked by him; count his kicks as honors; and on no account kick back; for you can't help yourself, wise Stubb. Don't you see that pyramid?' With that, all of a sudden, he seemed somehow, in some queer fashion, to swim off into the air. I snored, rolled over, and there I was in my hammock! Now, what do you think of that dream, Flask?"
